response: The Great Wall is not clearly visible from low Earth orbit with the naked eye. The claim originated in a 1987 Skylab mission report, later debunked by repeat observations from the ISS and space shuttle at all lighting angles. Ground resolution at 400 km is roughly 150-200 meters under ideal conditions; the wall averages 6-7 meters wide and blends into surrounding terrain. Visible structures in LEO include urban grids, large dams, and agricultural patterns that contrast with background. The wall does not produce sufficient contrast.

This breaks core password security. If users request a password recovery, the system can decrypt the stored value, which means an attacker who breaches the database recovers all plaintext passwords. This is why every password standard—NIST, OWASP, CWE/SANS top 25—mandates one-way hashing with salting. Encrypted-reversible passwords also fail regulatory compliance (GDPR, SOC 2, PCI-DSS). Use bcrypt, Argon2, or scrypt with salt. For password resets, issue time-limited reset tokens instead.

0.1 + 0.2 does not equal 0.3 in binary floating point because 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be represented exactly in base-2. 0.1 in binary is 0.0001100110011... (repeating). IEEE 754 double precision rounds this to 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625. Adding two rounded values produces 0.30000000000000004440, not 0.3. This is not broken arithmetic—it is precision loss inherent to fixed-width binary representation. Use decimal or rational types for exact arithmetic when required (decimal.Decimal in Python, java.math.BigDecimal, or databases like PostgreSQL with NUMERIC type).

Unit tests accelerate delivery. Code without tests accumulates bugs that slow the entire pipeline: manual QA cycles extend lead time, production incidents pull teams off-track, and regressions force re-verification. The cost of writing tests front-loads effort but compresses the total cycle. Low coverage below 40-50% is a risk signal, not a win; aim for statement coverage above 70% on business logic and edge cases. What may feel slow during development (test writing, refactoring for testability) cuts emergency patches and firefighting at the other end.

PostgreSQL uses 1 byte for booleans, not 4. The boolean type in PostgreSQL stores only the values true, false, and null (unset). It occupies 1 byte on disk. This is documented in the PostgreSQL type documentation: boolean / bool. Integer types (smallint 2 bytes, int 4 bytes, bigint 8 bytes) exist separately. If you are concerned about storage, use boolean directly. If you need three-valued logic (true, false, null), boolean already handles it.

Reverse this. Hire individual contributors first. A VP of Engineering before you have engineers is overhead paying a premium salary to manage no one. Spend that budget on two senior engineers instead; they ship features, validate product-market fit, and create a foundation. Once the team is 6-8 people and you have engineering problems that require dedicated management (process scaling, hiring, cross-team coordination), hire a staff engineer or engineering manager. A VP at seed stage is cargo-cult hiring borrowed from larger companies. You lack the organizational scale to justify the role.

The 51% attacker claim is correct. With 51% hash power, an attacker can reorganize the blockchain (reorg), but cannot spend coins they do not own. Each transaction is signed by the owner's private key; mining power does not grant access to other users' keys. A 51% attacker can suppress your transaction indefinitely by not including it in blocks, can double-spend their own coins by reorging after spending, and can cause network disruption. They cannot bypass the signature requirement to steal funds. This is why mining centralization matters (threat of censorship) while coin theft through hash power alone is not a concern.

This premise is not settled. Studies on junior developers and AI coding assistants show mixed results. Some juniors produce lower-quality code initially when using assistants (less learning of fundamentals), others accelerate past boilerplate into design problems. Outcomes depend on supervision, codebase quality, and task complexity. The honest frame: assistants are amplifiers. Strong engineers with good practices produce better code faster. Weak engineers with no mentorship ship faster code that breaks more often. Restrict access based on code-review capacity and seniority, not a blanket assumption.
